3.text:
With one endogenous regressor and $L=1$ instrument the first order Nagar
relative bias can be written on the OLS scale as

$$
{\rm RB}\;\approx\;\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
E\,F_{1}\approx 1+\mu^{2},
$$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$$
|{\rm RB}|\approx\frac1{F_{1}-1}\approx\frac1{F_{1}},\qquad 
|{\rm RB}|=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}|=10 .
$$

In the homoscedastic just identified limit

$$
L\,F_{1}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{L}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
F_{1}\approx \chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),
$$

and the usual Stock–Yogo weak instrument test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ versus $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects
$H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ when

$$
F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),
$$

$c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ being the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a
non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ $/\nu_{2}$.  On the
$\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit $c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ is the familiar
Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias critical value.  For $L=1$ and the
Nagar $10\%$ maximal relative bias

$$
\mu_{0}^{2}= \frac{L}{|{\rm RB}_{0}|}= \frac{1}{0.10}=10,
$$

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)=\hbox{ $0.95$-quantile of }
\chi^{2}_{1}(10)
\approx 16.38,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$.  In the textbook $E[{\rm RB}]\simeq
F_{1}^{-1}$ normalisation this is the usual $F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar
rule, $F_{1}\approx 1/|{\rm RB}|+1\approx11$, quoted in practice as the
$F>10$ rule of thumb.  The $16.4\approx16\!-\!17$ value is the
conventional $5\%$-size, i.e. $95\%$ confidence, Stock–Yogo implementation
of the $10\%$ Nagar relative bias criterion.

Remark.  On the crude normal approximation
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a genuine one-sided $95\%$
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ given an observed $f$ is
$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)\approx(\sqrt f-z_{0.95})^{2}$.  Imposing
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the sampling-error corrected inversion

$$
\sqrt{f_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95},\qquad 
f_{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1,
$$

$\approx26$ on the $z_{0.975}=1.96$ two-sided convention, the familiar
$F\approx20\!-\!30$ $95\%$ lower bound around the point estimate
$F\approx10$. ∎

4.text:
With a just identified homoskedastic model the Nagar first order
approximation is

${\rm E}\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta \approx 
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}$ , $L=1$,

so that on the OLS scale

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2}):=\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx
\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F\;,$

and $E\,F-1=\mu^{2}$ .  The $10\%$ relative bias point is therefore

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=1/0.10=10\;,$

the familiar $E|{\rm RB}|\approx1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar
rule, $F-1\approx11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ correction.

Inverting the weak IV test

$P\!\left(F_{1}\ge c\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right)=\alpha $

gives the usual Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias critical value.
With $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$  and $L=1$
$kF\sim\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ this is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a
non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$ .  In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$
limit

$c_{0.05}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)\approx 16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim 16.4$ rejects $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size and
can be read as $95\%$ confidence that $|{\rm RB}|<0.10$ in the Stock–Yogo
maximal-relative-bias sense.  This is the textbook $F>10$ rule with the
$5\%$ size correction, conventionally quoted as $F\gtrsim16\!-\!17$, the
point Nagar value being $F\approx1/b_{0}\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$.

Remark.  On the usual normal approximation
$\sqrt{F}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence
bound for the concentration parameter is
$\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$ with $z_{0.95}=1.645$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the conservative lower-confidence
inversion

$\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$,  $\approx26.2$ with the
conventional two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$, i.e. the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!30$
$95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar $1/F$ bias, $F\approx23\!-\!26$ on the
normal approximation, $F\approx23$ with $z_{0.95}$.  This is the $F>10$
rule inflated for the sampling variation of the first stage. ∎

8.text:
For $L=1$ the Nagar first order bias can be written on the OLS scale as

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm plim}\;{\rm bias}\big[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}\big]}
     {{\rm plim}\;{\rm bias}\big[\widehat\beta_{OLS}\big]}
     \;\approx\; \frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}},$

and, up to the $+1$, $\mu^{2}=E[F_{1}]-1\approx F_{1}$ under
homoscedasticity.  On the point Nagar approximation

${\rm RB}\approx F_{1}^{-1}\approx\big(F_{1}-1\big)^{-1},$

so that

${\rm RB}\approx0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}\approx L/b\approx10 $

and the familiar median-bias rule is $E[F_{1}]\approx1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$,
i.e. $F>10$.

Inverting the weak-instrument test for a $5\%$ size maximal relative bias
puts

$P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}=0.05,$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})/1$.  With $L=1$ and
$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10$ the $95\%$ quantile of the non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$ is

$c_{0.05}\!\left(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\right)
   \approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative-bias $5\%$ size critical value for
$k_{2}=1$.  Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16.4$ can be read as the usual $95\%$
confidence statement

${\rm P}\!\left\{{\rm RB}<0.10\mid F_{1}\ge c\right\}\approx0.95,$

i.e. the conventional conservative $10\%$ relative Nagar bias rule.
On the $1/F$ point Nagar form this is the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule,
$F\approx11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ correction, and $16.4\approx16$ is the
tabulated Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size version of it, often quoted as $F>17$.

Remark.  If the sampling variation of the first stage is put into the
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, the one-sided
$95\%$ lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=\big(\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$ gives
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10\iff \sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.

$F_{0.95}^{\,L}\approx\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx23.1,$

$\approx26$ on the $1.96$ two-sided normalisation, the usual $F\approx
20\!-\!30$ $95\%$ lower-bound inflation of the $F>10$ point rule. ∎

6.text:
With one instrument the first order Nagar relative bias on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\approx
(L-2)/\mu^{2}$, $L=1$, i.e.

${\rm RB}\approx -\mu^{-2}\approx-(F-1)^{-1}\approx-F^{-1} $

up to the usual $+1$ shift, so that on the Nagar scale

${\rm |RB|}<b\iff\mu^{2}>L/b $.

For $b=0.10$ and $L=1$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/b=10$

is the Nagar $10\%$ concentration.  In the homoskedastic just identified
limit

$LF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{L}(\mu^{2})$,

and for $L=1$

$F_{1}\approx\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$, $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\bigl(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\bigr)$.

The Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\;\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;{\rm |RB|}\ge b$

against $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects for

$F_{1}\ge c_{\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad
P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c_{\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}
=\alpha $,

i.e. $c_{\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a non–central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $\alpha=0.05$ and $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$

$c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)\approx 16.38$,

the usual Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal 2SLS relative bias critical value
for $L=1$.  On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the $5\%$
size, i.e. $95\%$ confidence, version of the textbook $E|{\rm RB}|
\approx 1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$ rule.  In practice this is quoted as
$F_{1}\gtrsim16{-}17$, $16.4\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, the
familiar $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the $z=0$ mean bias case.

Remark.  On the crude normal $\sqrt F$ approximation
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$ the one-sided
$95\%$ lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95})^{2}$ gives the
strict normal lower confidence inversion
$\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$ i.e.
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!26$ with the
usual $1.96$ two sided normalisation, $\approx26$, which is the
normal-approximate $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter around the $F\approx10$ point Nagar estimate.  The $16.4$
non-central $\chi^{2}$ value is the exact weak-instrument limit of the
same inversion and is the tabulated Stock–Yogo value normally used in
applied work.

2.text:
In the homoscedastic just identified model the Nagar first order bias can be
written on the OLS scale as

$${\rm RB}\equiv\frac{{\rm Bias}\big(\widehat\beta_{2SLS}\big)}
{{\rm Bias}\big(\widehat\beta_{OLS}\big)}
\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\qquad L=1, $$

so that up to the $F-1$ shift

$${\rm RB}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F ,
\qquad {\rm E}F\approx1+\mu^{2}, $$

and ${\rm RB}=0.10$ is the Nagar concentration

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b=1/0.10=10$ .

On the weak instrument limit
$F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ and with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$ .
The $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is therefore
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$ and

$\mu^{2}_{L}(F)\approx\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ .

Putting $\mu^{2}_{L}= \mu_{0}^{2}=10$ gives the usual square–root
inversion

$\sqrt F_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$F_{1-\alpha}\ge\big[\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}\big]^{2}$ .
With the one sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$F_{0.95}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,
$ \approx26$ on the conventional two-sided $1.96$ normalisation, i.e.
the familiar $F\approx20$–$30$ $95\%$ lower confidence version of the
text-book $F^{-1}$ rule $F\gtrsim1/b\approx10$.

In the conventional Stock–Yogo formulation the $5\%$ size test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects for $F\ge c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2})$,
$c_{0.95}$ being the $0.95$ quantile of a non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $L=1$ and $b=0.10$, $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$c_{0.95}\big(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\big)\approx 16.38$,

i.e. $F_{\rm 1st}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the usual Stock–Yogo
$5\%$ size, $10\%$ maximal relative bias, benchmark.  On the point
Nagar approximation this is the familiar $E[{\rm RB}]\approx F^{-1}<0.10\iff
F\gtrsim10$, the $16.4\approx16$ value being the conventional
$95\%$ size, maximal-relative-bias, $F>10$ rule of thumb.  This is the
$\approx 23$ normal lower bound $\,F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$ in the
$F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation.

12.text:
With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the first order Nagar
approximation under homoscedasticity is

${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\mid Z\big]\approx
\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\;\mu^{-2}$ , 
${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]\approx\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$ ,
and for $L=1$

$$
RB(\mu^{2})\;:=\;
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}
\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F  ,
\qquad \mu^{2}=\frac{\pi'Z'Z\pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}} .
$$

In the large $\nu_{2}$ limit

$$
F\stackrel{a}{\sim}1+\mu^{2},\qquad 
\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right) ,
$$

so that on the usual normal first-stage approximation

$\widehat\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ is the
$1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter.
For a $10\%$ Nagar relative bias we need

$$
\mu_{0}^{2}=\frac{L}{0.10}=10 ,
$$

and $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ is

$$
\sqrt{F}-z_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\sqrt{F}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}.
$$

With the one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$
\sqrt{F_{*}} \ge \sqrt{10}+1.645\approx 3.162+1.645=4.81,
$$

i.e.

$$
F_{*}\ge\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx 23\!-\!24,
$$

$F_{*}-1\approx 22$ on the $F-1$ Nagar normalisation,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the conventional two-sided
$1.96$ normalisation.  This is the $95\%$ one-sided lower-bound version
of the familiar point Nagar rule $ |RB|\approx1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$,
about $F\gtrsim11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ Nagar correction.

Remark.  On the Stock–Yogo 5$\%$ size maximal-relative-bias convention
the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$
is

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)\approx16.38\approx16,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\ge16\!-\!17$ is the tabulated $10\%$ maximal relative bias
$5\%$ size critical value, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the
$z=0$ limit of the expression above.  The $16.4$ number is the one
quoted in the Stock–Yogo tables; the $23\!-\!26$ numbers are the
explicit $95\%$ lower-confidence-bound inversion of the same Nagar
approximation. ∎

11.text:
With one endogenous regressor and one excluded instrument under
homoscedasticity

$ \mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ is the concentration
parameter and on the Nagar first order

${\rm E}[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta]\approx
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}},\qquad L=1,$

so that on the OLS bias scale

${\rm RB}\equiv
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\approx
\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
\mu^{2}\approx E\,F-1\approx F\;.$

In particular $|{\rm RB}|<0.10$ on the point Nagar scale is
$\mu^{2}>1/0.10=10$, i.e. $F-1>10$ or $F\gtrsim 11$, the familiar
$F>10$ rule.

Let $F_{1}$ be the usual first stage $F$.  For large $\nu_{2}$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ and

$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$.

Hence a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$
given an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt{f}-z_{0.95},\qquad z_{0.95}=1.645,$

so that, up to the $-1$ shift,

$\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\approx\bigl(\sqrt{f}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$ .
Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar relative bias to be
$<0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ with $\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10$,

$\sqrt{f_{0.95}}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{0.95}$,

$f_{0.95}\ge\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}\approx4.81^{2}\approx 23.1$,

essentially $f\approx23\!-\!24$.  With the usual $F-1$ Nagar
normalisation $\mu^{2}\approx F-1$ this is

$\sqrt{F-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\iff F\ge 1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}
\approx24.1$,

i.e. $F\approx 24$ for a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound on
$\mu^{2}$, $F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the conventional
two-sided $1.96$ normalisation.  This is the $F\approx10$ point Nagar
rule inflated by the sampling variation of the first stage.

In the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias language this is the test

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$,
$F_{1}\sim\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,

and the $5\%$ size critical value for maximal $|{\rm RB}|=0.10$,
$\mu_{0}^{2}=10$, is the $0.95$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$,

$c_{0.95}\approx 16.38$,

i.e. the familiar Stock–Yogo $F\gtrsim16\!-\!17$, conventionally quoted
as $F\approx16$, $F>10$ on the point Nagar $1/F$ approximation.  That
$16.4\approx16$ is the $5\%$ size maximal-bias table value most often
quoted as the “$95\%$ confident $10\%$ relative Nagar bias’’ rule, the
strict $95\%$ lower confidence bound on $\mu^{2}$ being the $F\approx
23\!-\!24$ figure above. ∎

10.text:
For $L=1$ endogenous regressor and $L=1$ instrument under homoscedasticity

$$
{\rm E}\big[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\mid Z\big]\simeq
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
\mu^{2}= \frac{\pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},
$$

so that on the OLS scale

$$
{\rm RB}\equiv 
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
 \simeq \frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx \frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}
 \approx\frac1F ,
\qquad E[F]=1+\mu^{2}.
$$

Hence on the point Nagar approximation

$$
|{\rm RB}|\simeq\mu^{-2}=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=10,
\qquad E[F]_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11,
$$

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule, $F-1\gtrsim10$.

Let $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$.  The Stock-Yogo
$5\%$ size test of

$$
H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\qquad{\rm vs}\qquad H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}
$$

rejects for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$, the $1-\alpha$ quantile
of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $|\rho_{0}|=0.10$ we have
$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/|\rho_{0}|=10$ and

$$
P\!\left(F_{1}\ge c_{0.95}\mid\mu^{2}=10\right)=0.05 .
$$

In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)=
q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}\!\left(10\right)\right]\approx 16.38,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the $5\%$ size, $95\%$ confidence,
maximal relative bias $10\%$ critical value.  With the usual $F\approx
\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the $F\gtrsim16$ Stock-Yogo $10\%$
maximal relative bias rule, the point Nagar $1/F$ rule being
$F^{*}\approx1/0.10=10$, $F^{*}-1\approx11$.

Remark.  On the asymptotic normalisation $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx
N\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big)$ a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound
for $\mu^{2}$ is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\big(\sqrt F-z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the normal-approximation lower bound

$$
\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645=4.81,
\qquad
F_{*}\approx23.1,
$$

$\approx26$ on the conventional $z_{0.975}=1.96$ two sided
convention, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower bound
about the textbook $F>10$ point estimate.  The $16.4\approx16$ value is
the Stock-Yogo tabulated $95\%$ confidence maximal relative bias
critical value normally quoted in applied work.

public_text.1:
The problem explicitly asks for the minimum F that delivers 95 % confidence the relative Nagar bias stays below 10 % under homoscedasticity. The Stock–Yogo tables are constructed precisely for that purpose: they invert the non-central χ² distribution (or its Nagar approximation) so that the probability the concentration parameter lies above the 10 % bias threshold equals 95 % when the observed F exceeds the tabulated critical value. For one endogenous regressor and one instrument that critical value is 16.38, which rounds to the nearest whole number 16.  

The derivations that produce 23 apply an extra normal approximation to the sampling distribution of F itself and then impose a one-sided 95 % lower bound on μ²; that step is already embedded in the Stock–Yogo inversion, so the additional layer double-counts the coverage requirement. The simpler point-estimate rule F > 10 likewise omits the coverage adjustment the problem requests. Therefore the operational threshold consistent with both the Nagar approximation and the stated 95 % confidence level remains the tabulated value of 16.
public_text.5: Colleagues 2/3/6/12/10/11 are right that the plain Nagar expansion gives a pointwise relative-bias threshold of roughly μ² = 10 (hence F ≈ 10–11) and that a normal lower-confidence adjustment on the concentration parameter alone pushes the number higher. The practical difficulty is that those calculations treat the first-stage F as if its only uncertainty is the sampling variation around a fixed μ²; they therefore double-count the variability that is already built into the Stock–Yogo maximal-bias tables. Those tables invert the non-central χ² exactly once, under the same homoscedastic Nagar approximation we are using, and deliver the 5 % critical value 16.38 for one instrument and a 10 % maximal relative bias. Any realized first-stage F above that tabulated threshold already guarantees, at the conventional 95 % coverage level, that the Nagar relative bias cannot exceed 10 %. Adding a second, separate normal inversion on top of the SY inversion simply produces an overly conservative number that practitioners have never adopted. The nearest whole number consistent with both the Nagar derivation and the published critical-value tables therefore remains 16.
public_text.14: The Stock-Yogo tabulation already supplies the exact 5 % critical value under the Nagar approximation and homoscedasticity for a single endogenous regressor and one instrument: 16.38 when the target is a maximal 10 % relative asymptotic bias. That number is obtained by inverting the non-central χ² distribution so that P(F > c | μ² = 10) = 0.95, which directly implements the 95 % guarantee the question asks for. The derivations that arrive at ≈23 are performing an extra normal lower-bound step on top of the already size-adjusted critical value; that step double-counts the sampling variability that the Stock-Yogo quantile has already incorporated. Consequently the tabulated 16.4, rounded to the nearest whole number, remains the appropriate threshold.
public_text.13: The Stock-Yogo tabulation for the Nagar approximation under homoscedasticity remains the most directly relevant benchmark here: with one endogenous regressor and one instrument, the critical value that keeps maximal relative asymptotic bias below 10 percent at the conventional 5 percent size is 16.38. Rounding to the nearest whole number therefore yields 16, and any first-stage F below that threshold leaves us unable to maintain 95 percent confidence that the bias ratio stays inside the target. The normal-inversion calculations that produce values near 23 or 26 are simply the one-sided lower-confidence-bound version of the same concentration-parameter requirement; they do not replace the tabulated threshold that already incorporates the size adjustment practitioners rely on. In applied work the 16.4 cutoff is the figure actually invoked for exactly this 10 percent bias / 95 percent statement, so the nearest whole number consistent with the standard reference is 16.
public_text.9:
The Stock–Yogo critical values are already constructed precisely for the 95 % coverage statement we need: they solve the non-centrality threshold that keeps the Nagar relative-bias term below 10 % with the conventional 5 % size adjustment, using the exact mapping from the first-stage F to the concentration parameter under homoscedasticity. For one endogenous regressor and one instrument that tabulated value is 16.38, which rounds to the nearest whole number 16.  

The derivations that arrive at 23–26 start from the same Nagar approximation but then layer an additional normal lower-bound inversion on top of the already size-adjusted critical value; that double-counts the uncertainty already embedded in the Stock–Yogo tables and produces an unnecessarily conservative threshold. In practice the pre-computed 16.4 benchmark is the number researchers are instructed to use when they want 95 % confidence that relative asymptotic bias stays under 10 %.
public_text.7:
Colleague 1 and several others have already laid out the case cleanly: under homoscedasticity and the Nagar approximation the Stock–Yogo tabulation for a single endogenous regressor and single instrument gives a critical value of 16.38 for keeping maximal relative bias below 10 percent at the conventional 5 percent size. That number is the one practitioners actually cite and the one that already embeds the 95 percent statement on the concentration parameter; any realized first-stage F below it leaves us unable to claim the desired bound.  

The derivations that arrive at ~23 start from the same Nagar setup but then layer an extra normal inversion on top of the already-tabulated quantile. That step effectively double-counts the sampling variability once the non-central χ² critical value has been computed, producing a more conservative threshold that is not the one reported in the Stock–Yogo tables or in the subsequent literature that relies on those tables. When the goal is a practical rule that matches the published benchmark, 16 remains the nearest whole number.  

I therefore continue to favor reporting 16.
public_text.3:
With one endogenous regressor and $L=1$ instrument the first order Nagar
relative bias can be written on the OLS scale as

$$
{\rm RB}\;\approx\;\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
E\,F_{1}\approx 1+\mu^{2},
$$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$$
|{\rm RB}|\approx\frac1{F_{1}-1}\approx\frac1{F_{1}},\qquad 
|{\rm RB}|=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}|=10 .
$$

In the homoscedastic just identified limit

$$
L\,F_{1}\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{L}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
F_{1}\approx \chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),
$$

and the usual Stock–Yogo weak instrument test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ versus $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects
$H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ when

$$
F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),
$$

$c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ being the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a
non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ $/\nu_{2}$.  On the
$\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit $c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ is the familiar
Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias critical value.  For $L=1$ and the
Nagar $10\%$ maximal relative bias

$$
\mu_{0}^{2}= \frac{L}{|{\rm RB}_{0}|}= \frac{1}{0.10}=10,
$$

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)=\hbox{ $0.95$-quantile of }
\chi^{2}_{1}(10)
\approx 16.38,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$.  In the textbook $E[{\rm RB}]\simeq
F_{1}^{-1}$ normalisation this is the usual $F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar
rule, $F_{1}\approx 1/|{\rm RB}|+1\approx11$, quoted in practice as the
$F>10$ rule of thumb.  The $16.4\approx16\!-\!17$ value is the
conventional $5\%$-size, i.e. $95\%$ confidence, Stock–Yogo implementation
of the $10\%$ Nagar relative bias criterion.

Remark.  On the crude normal approximation
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a genuine one-sided $95\%$
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ given an observed $f$ is
$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)\approx(\sqrt f-z_{0.95})^{2}$.  Imposing
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the sampling-error corrected inversion

$$
\sqrt{f_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95},\qquad 
f_{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1,
$$

$\approx26$ on the $z_{0.975}=1.96$ two-sided convention, the familiar
$F\approx20\!-\!30$ $95\%$ lower bound around the point estimate
$F\approx10$. ∎
public_text.4:
With a just identified homoskedastic model the Nagar first order
approximation is

${\rm E}\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta \approx 
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}$ , $L=1$,

so that on the OLS scale

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2}):=\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx
\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F\;,$

and $E\,F-1=\mu^{2}$ .  The $10\%$ relative bias point is therefore

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=1/0.10=10\;,$

the familiar $E|{\rm RB}|\approx1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar
rule, $F-1\approx11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ correction.

Inverting the weak IV test

$P\!\left(F_{1}\ge c\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right)=\alpha $

gives the usual Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias critical value.
With $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$  and $L=1$
$kF\sim\chi^{2}_{k}(\mu^{2})$ this is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a
non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$ .  In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$
limit

$c_{0.05}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)\approx 16.38\approx16\!-\!17$,

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim 16.4$ rejects $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size and
can be read as $95\%$ confidence that $|{\rm RB}|<0.10$ in the Stock–Yogo
maximal-relative-bias sense.  This is the textbook $F>10$ rule with the
$5\%$ size correction, conventionally quoted as $F\gtrsim16\!-\!17$, the
point Nagar value being $F\approx1/b_{0}\approx10$, $F-1\approx11$.

Remark.  On the usual normal approximation
$\sqrt{F}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence
bound for the concentration parameter is
$\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$ with $z_{0.95}=1.645$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the conservative lower-confidence
inversion

$\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$,  $\approx26.2$ with the
conventional two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$, i.e. the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!30$
$95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar $1/F$ bias, $F\approx23\!-\!26$ on the
normal approximation, $F\approx23$ with $z_{0.95}$.  This is the $F>10$
rule inflated for the sampling variation of the first stage. ∎
public_text.8:
For $L=1$ the Nagar first order bias can be written on the OLS scale as

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm plim}\;{\rm bias}\big[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}\big]}
     {{\rm plim}\;{\rm bias}\big[\widehat\beta_{OLS}\big]}
     \;\approx\; \frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}},$

and, up to the $+1$, $\mu^{2}=E[F_{1}]-1\approx F_{1}$ under
homoscedasticity.  On the point Nagar approximation

${\rm RB}\approx F_{1}^{-1}\approx\big(F_{1}-1\big)^{-1},$

so that

${\rm RB}\approx0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}\approx L/b\approx10 $

and the familiar median-bias rule is $E[F_{1}]\approx1+\mu_{0}^{2}\approx11$,
i.e. $F>10$.

Inverting the weak-instrument test for a $5\%$ size maximal relative bias
puts

$P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}=0.05,$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})/1$.  With $L=1$ and
$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10$ the $95\%$ quantile of the non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(10)$ is

$c_{0.05}\!\left(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\right)
   \approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17,$

the Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative-bias $5\%$ size critical value for
$k_{2}=1$.  Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16.4$ can be read as the usual $95\%$
confidence statement

${\rm P}\!\left\{{\rm RB}<0.10\mid F_{1}\ge c\right\}\approx0.95,$

i.e. the conventional conservative $10\%$ relative Nagar bias rule.
On the $1/F$ point Nagar form this is the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule,
$F\approx11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ correction, and $16.4\approx16$ is the
tabulated Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size version of it, often quoted as $F>17$.

Remark.  If the sampling variation of the first stage is put into the
lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\sim N(0,1)$, the one-sided
$95\%$ lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=\big(\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$ gives
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10\iff \sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.

$F_{0.95}^{\,L}\approx\big(\sqrt{10}+1.645\big)^{2}\approx23.1,$

$\approx26$ on the $1.96$ two-sided normalisation, the usual $F\approx
20\!-\!30$ $95\%$ lower-bound inflation of the $F>10$ point rule. ∎
public_text.6:
With one instrument the first order Nagar relative bias on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\approx
(L-2)/\mu^{2}$, $L=1$, i.e.

${\rm RB}\approx -\mu^{-2}\approx-(F-1)^{-1}\approx-F^{-1} $

up to the usual $+1$ shift, so that on the Nagar scale

${\rm |RB|}<b\iff\mu^{2}>L/b $.

For $b=0.10$ and $L=1$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/b=10$

is the Nagar $10\%$ concentration.  In the homoskedastic just identified
limit

$LF\;\xrightarrow{d}\;\chi^{2}_{L}(\mu^{2})$,

and for $L=1$

$F_{1}\approx\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$, $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\bigl(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\bigr)$.

The Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\;\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;{\rm |RB|}\ge b$

against $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects for

$F_{1}\ge c_{\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad
P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c_{\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}
=\alpha $,

i.e. $c_{\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a non–central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $\alpha=0.05$ and $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$

$c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)\approx 16.38$,

the usual Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal 2SLS relative bias critical value
for $L=1$.  On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the $5\%$
size, i.e. $95\%$ confidence, version of the textbook $E|{\rm RB}|
\approx 1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$ rule.  In practice this is quoted as
$F_{1}\gtrsim16{-}17$, $16.4\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, the
familiar $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the $z=0$ mean bias case.

Remark.  On the crude normal $\sqrt F$ approximation
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$ the one-sided
$95\%$ lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}=(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95})^{2}$ gives the
strict normal lower confidence inversion
$\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$ i.e.
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!26$ with the
usual $1.96$ two sided normalisation, $\approx26$, which is the
normal-approximate $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter around the $F\approx10$ point Nagar estimate.  The $16.4$
non-central $\chi^{2}$ value is the exact weak-instrument limit of the
same inversion and is the tabulated Stock–Yogo value normally used in
applied work.
public_text.2:
In the homoscedastic just identified model the Nagar first order bias can be
written on the OLS scale as

$${\rm RB}\equiv\frac{{\rm Bias}\big(\widehat\beta_{2SLS}\big)}
{{\rm Bias}\big(\widehat\beta_{OLS}\big)}
\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\qquad L=1, $$

so that up to the $F-1$ shift

$${\rm RB}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F ,
\qquad {\rm E}F\approx1+\mu^{2}, $$

and ${\rm RB}=0.10$ is the Nagar concentration

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b=1/0.10=10$ .

On the weak instrument limit
$F\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ and with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$ .
The $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is therefore
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}\approx\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}$ and

$\mu^{2}_{L}(F)\approx\bigl(\sqrt F-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ .

Putting $\mu^{2}_{L}= \mu_{0}^{2}=10$ gives the usual square–root
inversion

$\sqrt F_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$F_{1-\alpha}\ge\big[\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}\big]^{2}$ .
With the one sided $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$F_{0.95}\approx\big[\sqrt{10}+1.645\big]^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,
$ \approx26$ on the conventional two-sided $1.96$ normalisation, i.e.
the familiar $F\approx20$–$30$ $95\%$ lower confidence version of the
text-book $F^{-1}$ rule $F\gtrsim1/b\approx10$.

In the conventional Stock–Yogo formulation the $5\%$ size test of
$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects for $F\ge c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2})$,
$c_{0.95}$ being the $0.95$ quantile of a non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $L=1$ and $b=0.10$, $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$c_{0.95}\big(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\big)\approx 16.38$,

i.e. $F_{\rm 1st}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the usual Stock–Yogo
$5\%$ size, $10\%$ maximal relative bias, benchmark.  On the point
Nagar approximation this is the familiar $E[{\rm RB}]\approx F^{-1}<0.10\iff
F\gtrsim10$, the $16.4\approx16$ value being the conventional
$95\%$ size, maximal-relative-bias, $F>10$ rule of thumb.  This is the
$\approx 23$ normal lower bound $\,F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}$ in the
$F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation.
public_text.12:
With one endogenous regressor and one instrument the first order Nagar
approximation under homoscedasticity is

${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\mid Z\big]\approx
\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\;\mu^{-2}$ , 
${\rm E}\big[\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta\big]\approx\sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}$ ,
and for $L=1$

$$
RB(\mu^{2})\;:=\;
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\approx\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}
\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F  ,
\qquad \mu^{2}=\frac{\pi'Z'Z\pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}} .
$$

In the large $\nu_{2}$ limit

$$
F\stackrel{a}{\sim}1+\mu^{2},\qquad 
\sqrt F\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right) ,
$$

so that on the usual normal first-stage approximation

$\widehat\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$ is the
$1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter.
For a $10\%$ Nagar relative bias we need

$$
\mu_{0}^{2}=\frac{L}{0.10}=10 ,
$$

and $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}$ is

$$
\sqrt{F}-z_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
\sqrt{F}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}.
$$

With the one-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$$
\sqrt{F_{*}} \ge \sqrt{10}+1.645\approx 3.162+1.645=4.81,
$$

i.e.

$$
F_{*}\ge\Bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\Bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1\approx 23\!-\!24,
$$

$F_{*}-1\approx 22$ on the $F-1$ Nagar normalisation,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$ on the conventional two-sided
$1.96$ normalisation.  This is the $95\%$ one-sided lower-bound version
of the familiar point Nagar rule $ |RB|\approx1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$,
about $F\gtrsim11$ with the $1/(F-1)$ Nagar correction.

Remark.  On the Stock–Yogo 5$\%$ size maximal-relative-bias convention
the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$
is

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)\approx16.38\approx16,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\ge16\!-\!17$ is the tabulated $10\%$ maximal relative bias
$5\%$ size critical value, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the
$z=0$ limit of the expression above.  The $16.4$ number is the one
quoted in the Stock–Yogo tables; the $23\!-\!26$ numbers are the
explicit $95\%$ lower-confidence-bound inversion of the same Nagar
approximation. ∎

$$
{\rm E}\big[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\mid Z\big]\simeq
\frac{\sigma_{uv}}{\sigma_{v}^{2}}\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}},\qquad 
\mu^{2}= \frac{\pi^{\prime}Z^{\prime}Z\pi}{\sigma_{v}^{2}},
$$

so that on the OLS scale

$$
{\rm RB}\equiv 
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
 \simeq \frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx \frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}
 \approx\frac1F ,
\qquad E[F]=1+\mu^{2}.
$$

Hence on the point Nagar approximation

$$
|{\rm RB}|\simeq\mu^{-2}=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=10,
\qquad E[F]_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11,
$$

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule, $F-1\gtrsim10$.

Let $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$.  The Stock-Yogo
$5\%$ size test of

$$
H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\qquad{\rm vs}\qquad H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}
$$

rejects for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$, the $1-\alpha$ quantile
of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $|\rho_{0}|=0.10$ we have
$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/|\rho_{0}|=10$ and

$$
P\!\left(F_{1}\ge c_{0.95}\mid\mu^{2}=10\right)=0.05 .
$$

In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$$
c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)=
q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}\!\left(10\right)\right]\approx 16.38,
$$

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the $5\%$ size, $95\%$ confidence,
maximal relative bias $10\%$ critical value.  With the usual $F\approx
\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the $F\gtrsim16$ Stock-Yogo $10\%$
maximal relative bias rule, the point Nagar $1/F$ rule being
$F^{*}\approx1/0.10=10$, $F^{*}-1\approx11$.

Remark.  On the asymptotic normalisation $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx
N\big(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\big)$ a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound
for $\mu^{2}$ is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\big(\sqrt F-z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the normal-approximation lower bound

$$
\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\approx3.162+1.645=4.81,
\qquad
F_{*}\approx23.1,
$$

$\approx26$ on the conventional $z_{0.975}=1.96$ two sided
convention, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower bound
about the textbook $F>10$ point estimate.  The $16.4\approx16$ value is
the Stock-Yogo tabulated $95\%$ confidence maximal relative bias
critical value normally quoted in applied work.

4.text:
For a just identified homoscedastic model with $L=1$ the Nagar first order
relative bias on the OLS scale is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\bigl(F-1\bigr)^{-1}
\simeq F^{-1}$,

$E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$, so on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<0.10\iff \mu^{2}>1/0.10=10\iff F-1>10$, 
i.e. the familiar $F\gtrsim10\!-\!11$ point rule.

Let $F_{1}$ be the first stage $F$.  In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ ,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$,

and the Stock-Yogo weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10\;\;\;{\rm vs}\;\;\;
H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects $H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ for

$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad 
P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}=\alpha,$

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of 
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With the $10\%$ Nagar bias

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}_{0}|=1/0.10=10$.

Hence on the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]\approx16.38$,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size.
That is the conventional $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative
Nagar bias, Stock-Yogo benchmark, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the
$z=0$ limit of the same inversion.  In applied practice this is quoted as
the $F>10$ rule with the $5\%$ size correction $F\gtrsim16$, 
$16.38\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, $\approx17$ on the usual
round-up convention.

Remark.  On the crude normal approximation 
$\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$ the one sided $95\%$
lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter is
$\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10\iff\sqrt{F}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $F_{*}-1\approx24.1$ on the
$F-1$ Nagar normalisation, $\approx26$ with the conventional $z_{0.975}=1.96$
two sided normalisation.  This is the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative
$95\%$ lower-bound inflation of the textbook $F\gtrsim10$ point rule; the
$16.4\approx16$ value is the Stock-Yogo tabulated $5\%$ size maximal
relative bias critical value normally used for the “$95\%$ confident
$10\%$ relative bias’’ statement. ∎

11.text:
The Nagar first order under homoscedasticity with $L=1$

${\rm E}[\hat\beta_{2SLS}-\beta\mid Z]\simeq \sigma_{uv}\sigma_{v}^{-2}\,
\frac{L-2}{\mu^{2}}$,

so on the OLS bias scale

${\rm RB}\equiv\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\simeq
\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{\mu^{2}}\approx\frac1{F-1}\approx\frac1F,
\qquad E[F]=1+\mu^{2}$.

Point Nagar 
$|{\rm RB}|=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=L/0.10=10\iff E[F]_{0}\simeq1+10=11$,
the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,
$P\{F_{1}\ge c\mid\mu^{2}\}=1-F_{\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})}(c)$.

The Stock–Yogo weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff |{\rm RB}|\ge 0.10$
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$,
$c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
With the $10\%$ Nagar target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)=q_{0.95}\big[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\big]\approx16.38$.

Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16.4$ is the $5\%$ size, i.e. $95\%$ confidence,
maximal-relative-bias $10\%$ critical value, conventionally quoted as
$F>16\!-\!17$, the $F\approx10\!-\!11$ point Nagar value being the
$z=0$ limit of the inversion.

Remark.  On the normalisation $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a
one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter
is $\mu_{L}^{2}(f)=\big(\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\big)^{2}$. Imposing
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the strict normal lower-bound inversion
$\sqrt{f_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$f_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $\approx26$ with
$z_{0.975}=1.96$, i.e. the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative lower bound
around the textbook $F>10$ point rule. The tabulated Stock–Yogo value
$16.38\approx16$ is the value actually used in applied work for the
$95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias rule.

Under homoscedasticity with $L=1$

${\rm RB}\equiv{\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\simeq L/\mu^{2}

10.text:
Under homoscedasticity with $L=1$ and the Nagar first order

${\rm RB}\equiv{\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\approx L/\mu^{2}

${\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2}$.  On the point Nagar scale

\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$ rejects for

$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$,

$c_{0.95}\bigl(\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\bigr)\approx16.38$,

so that in the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the

12.text:
For $L=1$ the first order Nagar approximation under homoscedasticity can be
written on the OLS scale as

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\equiv
\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}\simeq \frac{L}{\mu^{2}}
\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{F-1}\simeq\frac1F$

with $E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$ and $\mu^{2}= \pi'Z'Z\pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$.  On the
point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff \mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$,

so that for a $10\%$ relative bias

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=1/0.10=10 $
is the Nagar $10\%$ concentration and on the mean scale
$E\,F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$, the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ and for large $\nu_{2}$ 

$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$

so that a one-sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$
given an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad
\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\approx\bigl(\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}.$

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar relative bias to be
$<0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt f_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$f_{1-\alpha}\ge\bigl[\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}.$

With the one-sided normal $z_{0.95}=1.645$

$\sqrt{f_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$

and

$f_{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$

on the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation.  With the usual Nagar
$F-1$ shift $\mu^{2}\approx F-1$,

$\sqrt{F_{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,

$F_{*}\ge1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

i.e. the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower bound
about the textbook $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule.  On the conventional
two sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation this is
$f_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26$.

Remark.  In the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size maximal-relative-bias
convention the $1-\alpha$ quantile of a non-central
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$ is

$c_{0.95}\bigl(\mu_{0}^{2}=10\bigr)=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx16.38\approx16$,

i.e. $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ is the tabulated Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size,
$95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative bias critical value most
often quoted in applied work as the $F>10$ rule, the $16.4\approx16$
value being the $z=0$ limit of the normal lower bound above. ∎

For a just identified homoscedastic model with $L=1$ the Nagar first order
relative bias on the OLS scale is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq\bigl(F-1\bigr)^{-1}
\simeq F^{-1}$,

$E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$, so on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<0.10\iff \mu^{2}>1/0.10=10\iff F-1>10$, 
i.e. the familiar $F\gtrsim10\!-\!11$ point rule.

Let $F_{1}$ be the first stage $F$.  In the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$ ,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$,

and the Stock-Yogo weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10\;\;\;{\rm vs}\;\;\;
H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects $H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ for

$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad 
P\!\left\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\right\}=\alpha,$

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of 
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With the $10\%$ Nagar bias

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}_{0}|=1/0.10=10$.

Hence on the $\nu_{2}\to\infty$ limit

$c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]\approx16.38$,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size.
That is the conventional $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative
Nagar bias, Stock-Yogo benchmark, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule being the
$z=0$ limit of the same inversion.  In applied practice this is quoted as
the $F>10$ rule with the $5\%$ size correction $F\gtrsim16$, 
$16.38\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, $\approx17$ on the usual
round-up convention.

Remark.  On the crude normal approximation 
$\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=\bigl(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$ the one sided $95\%$
lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter is
$\mu_{L}^{2}\ge10\iff\sqrt{F}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$, i.e.
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $F_{*}-1\approx24.1$ on the
$F-1$ Nagar normalisation, $\approx26$ with the conventional $z_{0.975}=1.96$
two sided normalisation.  This is the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative
$95\%$ lower-bound inflation of the textbook $F\gtrsim10$ point rule; the
$16.4\approx16$ value is the Stock-Yogo tabulated $5\%$ size maximal
relative bias critical value normally used for the “$95\%$ confident
$10\%$ relative bias’’ statement. ∎

With $L=1$ and homoscedasticity the Nagar first order relative bias on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RB}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
$\qquad E F =1+\mu^{2}$,

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|_{0}=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}|_{0}=10$,

$E F_{0}\simeq1+10=11$, the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,

and the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test is

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ 
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$,

rejected at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ with

$P\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\}=\alpha$,

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
For the 10% Nagar target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)=q_{0.95}\big[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\big]\approx16.38$.

Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size, i.e. it
is the $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias critical value.
On the $E\,{\rm RB}\simeq F^{-1}$ normalisation this is the textbook
$F>10$ rule with the $5\%$ size correction, conventionally quoted as
$F\approx16$, $16.38\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, $\approx17$ on
the usual round-up convention.

The normal lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$ gives the
strict $95\%$ lower confidence inversion $\sqrt F_{*}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $\approx24$ on the $F-1$
normalisation, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative inflation of the point
$F\approx10$ rule.  That second inversion is already embodied in the
non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile $q_{0.95}[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)]$; layering it on
top double counts the sampling variability of $F$.  The tabulated
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias value is the operational
$95\%$ guarantee used in applied work.

3.text:
Under homoscedasticity with $L=1$ the first order Nagar relative bias on the
OLS scale is

${\rm RB}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
$\qquad E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$,

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|_{0}=0.10\iff\mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}|_{0}=10$,

$E F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$, the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,

and the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le \mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$
versus $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$,
$c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ the $1-\alpha$ quantile of
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  For the 10 % Nagar target
$\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}\bigl[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\bigr]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx 16.38$,

i.e. $P\{F_{1}\ge c_{0.95}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.95$.  Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim
16\!-\!17$ is the $5\%$ size, 95 % confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative
Nagar bias critical value.  In the usual $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation
this is the tabulated Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias rule,
conventionally quoted as $F>10$ on the point $1/F$ approximation and
$F\approx16.4\approx16$ with the $5\%$ size correction.  Rounded up for
a strict $>$ inequality the operational benchmark is $F\gtrsim17$.

Remark.  On the crude normal approximation $\sqrt{F}\approx
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the
concentration parameter is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=(\sqrt{F}-z_{0.95})^{2}$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the strict lower-bound inversion
$\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!24$ on the
$F-1$ Nagar normalisation, $\approx26$ with $z_{0.975}=1.96$, the
$F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative inflation of the point $F\approx10$
Nagar rule.  The $16.38\approx16$ non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile is the
exact weak-instrument limit of the Stock–Yogo inversion that is tabulated
and used in practice for the stated $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal
relative bias statement.

8.text:
With $L=1$ homoscedastic Nagar first order

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\simeq L/\mu^{2}
\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$, 
$E F =1+\mu^{2}$.

On the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<0.10\iff \mu^{2}>L/0.10=10$,

$E F_{0}\simeq1+10=11$ the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$.

The weak instrument test of maximal relative Nagar bias

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff |{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ 
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$, 
$c_{1-\alpha}$ the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
With the $10\%$ Nagar target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}\bigl[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\bigr]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx16.38$.

Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16.4$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size, i.e. the
conventional $95\%$ confidence $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias
Stock–Yogo benchmark. On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is
the tabulated $F\approx16\!-\!17$ rule, the $F>10$ point Nagar value
being the $z=0$ limit.

Remark on the strict normal lower bound. On $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$
the one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound is 
$\mu_{L}^{2}(f)=\bigl(\sqrt f-z_{0.95}\bigr)^{2}$. 
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives

$\sqrt{f_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$f_{*}\ge\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1$,

$\approx24$ on the $F-1$ normalisation, $\approx26$ with $z_{0.975}=1.96$,
the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower bound inflation of the
textbook $F\approx10$ point rule. The $16.38\approx16$ non-central
$\chi^{2}$ quantile is the Stock–Yogo tabulated operational threshold
that is used in applied work for the stated $95\%$ confident $10\%$
maximal relative bias claim.

2.text:
For $L=1$ homoscedastic first stage

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\simeq L/\mu^{2}
\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1} , \qquad 
{\rm E}F=1+\mu^{2} ,$

$\mu^{2}= \pi'Z'Z\pi/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ is the concentration parameter. On the
point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|=b_{0}\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}$

so that for the 10% relative bias target

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10,\qquad {\rm E}F_{0}\simeq1+10=11,$

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.  In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1),$

and the weak instrument test of

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10\quad{\rm vs}\quad 
H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ where
$c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
With $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$c_{0.95}\big[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\big]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx 16.38 $

is the $5\%$ size critical value.  Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16.4$ rejects
$\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. $|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$, at $5\%$ size, the conventional
$95\%$ confidence $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias benchmark.  On the
$F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the tabulated Stock–Yogo
$10\%$ maximal relative bias rule, conventionally quoted as $F>10$ on the
point scale and $F\approx16\!-\!17$ with the $5\%$ size correction,
$16.38\approx16$ to the nearest integer, $\approx17$ on the usual round-up
convention.  The $E F\approx11$ point Nagar $F\approx10$ rule is the
$z=0$ limit of the inversion.

Remark.  On the crude normalisation $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$
the one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=
(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$ gives the strict normal lower bound inversion
$\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$, i.e. $F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}
\approx23.1$, $\approx24$ on the $F-1$ Nagar shift and $\approx26$ with
$z_{0.975}=1.96$, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative inflation of the
point $F\approx10$ rule.  The $16.4$ non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile is the
exact weak-instrument Stock–Yogo inversion normally used in applied work
for the $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal relative bias statement.

11.text:
With one endogenous regressor and $L=1$ the first order Nagar relative
bias on the OLS scale under homoscedasticity is

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\simeq
L/\mu^{2}\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
$E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$.

On the point Nagar scale
$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff\mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$ so that for $b_{0}=0.10$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=10$,
$E F_{0}\approx1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$, 
the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit
$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,
$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right)$,
and the Stock–Yogo maximal-relative-bias test is

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$,

reject $H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ for
$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ where
$c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of
$\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.  With $\alpha=0.05$ and $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$

$c_{0.95}\big[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\big]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\right]
\approx16.38$ .

Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size,
i.e. it is the $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias
critical value.  On the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is the
tabulated Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative bias benchmark,
conventionally quoted as $F>10$ with the $5\%$ size correction
$F\approx16$.  Rounded to the nearest whole number $16.38\approx16$,
$\approx17$ on the usual round-up convention.

Remark.  On the crude normalisation $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$
a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration
parameter is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)\approx(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$.
Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the normal-approximate strict lower
bound
$\sqrt{F_{*}}=\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!24$,
$\approx26$ with $z_{0.975}=1.96$, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative
inflation of the point $F\approx10$ Nagar rule.  The $16.38\approx16$
non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile is the exact weak-instrument limit of
the inversion and is the value tabulated by Stock–Yogo and used in
practice for the $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal relative bias
statement. ∎

10.text:
For $L=1$ and homoscedasticity the first-order Nagar relative bias on the
OLS scale is

${\rm RB}(\mu^{2})\simeq L\mu^{-2}\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq
F^{-1},\qquad E[F]=1+\mu^{2},$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff\mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$.

With $b_{0}=0.10$ and $L=1$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10,\qquad E[F]_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11,$

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2}),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1\right),$

and the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test of

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff |{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects $H_{0}$ at size $\alpha$ for

$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad
P\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\}=\alpha,$

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
For the $10\%$ Nagar target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}\bigl[\chi_{1}^{2}(10)\bigr]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi_{1}^{2}(10)\right]
\approx 16.38,$

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim16$–$17$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size.
That is the conventional $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar
bias critical value that is tabulated by Stock–Yogo and quoted in applied
work as the $F>10$ rule with the $5\%$ size correction.  On the
$F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation this is $F\approx16.4\approx16$, $E[F]_{0}
\approx11$ on the $F-1$ Nagar normalisation, i.e. the usual $\approx 16$,
often reported as $F>17$ on the strict round-up convention.

Remark.  On the crude normalisation $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ the
one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the concentration parameter is
$\mu_{L}^{2}(F)\approx(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$.  Imposing
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the strict normal lower-bound inversion

$\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95},\qquad 
F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23\!-\!24$

on the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation, $\approx24$ on the $F-1$ shift and
$\approx26$ with the conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$.  That is the
$F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower-bound inflation of the point
$F\approx10$ Nagar rule.  The $16.38\approx16$ non-central $\chi^{2}$
quantile is the exact weak-instrument limit of the same inversion and is
the operational Stock–Yogo $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal relative bias
benchmark. ∎

12.text:
Under homoscedasticity with $L=1$ the first–order Nagar result on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RB}\equiv {\rm bias}_{2SLS}/{\rm bias}_{OLS}\simeq L/\mu^{2}
\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq(F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1},\qquad 
E\,F=1+\mu^{2},$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff\mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$.

For $b_{0}=0.10$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=10$, $E F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$, 
the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,

and the Stock–Yogo weak instrument test

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>
\mu_{0}^{2}$

rejects at size $\alpha$ for

$F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2}),\qquad 
P\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\}=\alpha,$

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
With the Nagar $10\%$ target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}\bigl[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\bigr]\approx16.38,$

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim16$–$17$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size.  In the
applied literature this is read as the $95\%$–confidence, $10\%$ maximal
relative Nagar bias rule, viz. the tabulated Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal
relative bias critical value.  On the $1/F$ normalisation this is the
textbook $F\gtrsim10$, $F-1\gtrsim10$, point Nagar rule with the $5\%$
size correction, conventionally quoted as $F>16$, $16.38\approx16$ to the
nearest whole number, $\approx17$ on the usual round-up convention.

Remark.  On the asymptotic normalisation $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ a one-sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound for
$\mu^{2}$ is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$.  Imposing
$\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the strict normal lower-bound inversion

$\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95},\qquad 
F_{*}\ge\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1,$

$\,F_{*}-1\approx24.1$ on the $F-1$ Nagar normalisation and $\approx26$
with the conventional $z_{0.975}=1.96$, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$
conservative inflation of the point $F\approx10$ Nagar rule.  The
$16.4\approx16$ non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile is the exact
weak-instrument limit of the inversion and is the Stock–Yogo value that
is actually used in practice for the $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal
relative bias statement. ∎

4.text:
For $L=1$ under homoscedasticity

${\rm RB}\equiv\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{F-1}\simeq\frac1F$,
$\qquad E F=1+\mu^{2},$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff \mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$.

For a $10\%$ relative bias $b_{0}=0.10$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=10$,
$E F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar rule.

In the weak instrument limit $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
and for $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\,1\right) $

so that a one-sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ given an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad
\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\approx\big(\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\big)^{2}$.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar relative bias to be
$<0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt f_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

$f_{1-\alpha}\ge\bigl[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\bigr]^{2}$.

With the one-sided normal $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{f_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

$f_{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,
on the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation.  On the Nagar $F-1$ normalisation
$\mu^{2}\approx F-1$,

$\sqrt{F_{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,
$F_{*}\ge1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

i.e. the usual $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower-bound
inflation of the textbook $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule.  With the
conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $\approx26$.

Remark.  The operational Stock–Yogo $5\%$-size maximal-relative-bias
control that is tabulated in the weak-instrument literature is the
$1-\alpha$ quantile of the non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$,

$c_{0.95}\bigl[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\bigr]\approx16.38\approx16$,

so that $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le10\iff|{\rm RB}|
\ge0.10$ at $5\%$ size, the $F>10$ rule with its $5\%$ size correction
normally quoted as the $95\%$ confident $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar
bias benchmark.  That is the $16.38\approx16$ value used in applied
practice. ∎

Colleagues 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11, 13 and 14 have already shown that the Stock–Yogo construction directly inverts the non-central χ²₁(10) under the homoscedastic Nagar approximation permitted by the problem. That inversion yields the exact 5 % size critical value 16.38, so any realized first-stage F above the tabulated threshold already supplies the required 95 % statement that relative asymptotic bias stays below 10 %.  

The normal lower-bound calculation that produces ≈23 simply reapplies the 95 % coverage requirement after the non-central quantile has already incorporated the sampling variability of F; the result is therefore an extra layer of conservatism that does not appear in the published Stock–Yogo tables and is not used in applied work. Because the problem asks for the conventional 95 % guarantee under the Nagar/Stock–Yogo framework, the tabulated value rounded to the nearest whole number—16—remains the minimum F that meets the stated criterion. Any argument for 23 would require discarding the single, pre-computed inversion that practitioners actually rely on for this exact statement.

public_text.6:
With $L=1$ and homoscedasticity the Nagar first order relative bias on the OLS
scale is

${\rm RB}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq \mu^{-2}\simeq (F-1)^{-1}\simeq F^{-1}$,
$\qquad E F =1+\mu^{2}$,

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|_{0}=0.10\iff \mu_{0}^{2}=L/|{\rm RB}|_{0}=10$,

$E F_{0}\simeq1+10=11$, the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$,

and the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test is

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ 
vs $H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$,

rejected at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ with

$P\{F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}\mid\mu^{2}=\mu_{0}^{2}\}=\alpha$,

i.e. $c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
For the 10% Nagar target $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$ and $\alpha=0.05$

$c_{0.95}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)=q_{0.95}\big[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)\big]\approx16.38$.

Hence $F_{1}\gtrsim16\!-\!17$ rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$ at $5\%$ size, i.e. it
is the $95\%$ confidence, $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias critical value.

$F>10$ rule with the $5\%$ size correction, conventionally quoted as
$F\approx16$, $16.38\approx16$ to the nearest whole number, $\approx17$ on
the usual round-up convention.

The normal lower bound $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)=(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$ gives the
strict $95\%$ lower confidence inversion $\sqrt F_{*}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $\approx24$ on the $F-1$
normalisation, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative inflation of the point
$F\approx10$ rule.  That second inversion is already embodied in the
non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile $q_{0.95}[\chi^{2}_{1}(10)]$; layering it on
top double counts the sampling variability of $F$.  The tabulated
Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size $10\%$ maximal relative bias value is the operational
$95\%$ guarantee used in applied work.

For $L=1$ under homoscedasticity

${\rm RB}\equiv\frac{{\rm bias}_{2SLS}}{{\rm bias}_{OLS}}
\simeq\frac{L}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{F-1}\simeq\frac1F$,
$\qquad E F=1+\mu^{2},$

so that on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff \mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$.

For a $10\%$ relative bias $b_{0}=0.10$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=L/b_{0}=10$,
$E F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point Nagar rule.

In the weak instrument limit $F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$
and for $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx N\!\left(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},\,1\right) $

so that a one-sided $1-\alpha$ lower confidence bound for
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ given an observed $f$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}_{L}(f)=\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad
\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\approx\big(\sqrt f-z_{1-\alpha}\big)^{2}$.

Requiring the $95\%$ lower bound for the Nagar relative bias to be
$<0.10$, i.e. $\mu^{2}_{L}(f)\ge\mu_{0}^{2}=10$,

$\sqrt f_{1-\alpha}\ge\sqrt{\mu_{0}^{2}}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

$f_{1-\alpha}\ge\bigl[\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}\bigr]^{2}$.

With the one-sided normal $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{f_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645\approx3.162+1.645=4.81$,

$f_{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1\approx23$,
on the $F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation.  On the Nagar $F-1$ normalisation
$\mu^{2}\approx F-1$,

$\sqrt{F_{*}-1}\ge\sqrt{10}+1.645$,
$F_{*}\ge1+\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx24.1\approx24$,

i.e. the usual $F\approx20\!-\!30$ conservative $95\%$ lower-bound
inflation of the textbook $F\approx10$ point Nagar rule.  With the
conventional two-sided $z_{0.975}=1.96$ this is $\approx26$.

Remark.  The operational Stock–Yogo $5\%$-size maximal-relative-bias
control that is tabulated in the weak-instrument literature is the
$1-\alpha$ quantile of the non-central $\chi^{2}_{1}(\mu_{0}^{2}=10)$,

With $L=1$ under homoscedasticity the first order Nagar relative bias on the
OLS scale is

${\rm RB}\simeq L/\mu^{2}\simeq\mu^{-2}$, $\;E\,F=1+\mu^{2}$,

so on the point Nagar scale

$|{\rm RB}|<b_{0}\iff\mu^{2}>L/b_{0}$.

For $b_{0}=0.10$,

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/0.10=10$,     $E F_{0}\simeq1+\mu_{0}^{2}=11$,

the familiar $F\gtrsim10$ point rule.

In the weak instrument limit with $\nu_{2}\to\infty$

$F_{1}\stackrel{a}{\sim}\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$,  $\sqrt{F_{1}}\approx
N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$,

and the Stock–Yogo maximal relative bias test is

$H_{0}:\mu^{2}\le\mu_{0}^{2}\iff|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$ vs
$H_{1}:\mu^{2}>\mu_{0}^{2}$,

rejected at size $\alpha$ for $F_{1}\ge c_{1-\alpha}(\mu_{0}^{2})$ where
$c_{1-\alpha}$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu_{0}^{2})$.
With $\alpha=0.05$ and $\mu_{0}^{2}=10$

$c_{0.95}\big[\chi_{1}^{2}(10)\big]=q_{0.95}\!\left[\chi_{1}^{2}(10)\right]
\approx16.38$ .

Hence $P\{F_{1}\ge c_{0.95}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.95$ and $F_{1}\gtrsim16$–$17$
rejects $\mu^{2}\le10$, i.e. $|{\rm RB}|\ge0.10$, at $5\%$ size.  This is the
tabulated Stock–Yogo $10\%$ maximal relative Nagar bias $95\%$ confidence
critical value, conventionally quoted as $F\approx16.4\approx16$ on the
$F\approx\mu^{2}$ normalisation, $ \approx17$ on the usual strict round-up
convention, the $F>10$ point Nagar rule with its $5\%$ size correction.

Remark.  On the crude normalisation $\sqrt F\approx N(\sqrt{\mu^{2}},1)$ the
one sided $95\%$ lower confidence bound is $\mu_{L}^{2}(F)\approx
(\sqrt F-z_{0.95})^{2}$.  Imposing $\mu_{L}^{2}=10$ gives the strict normal
lower-bound inversion $\sqrt{F_{*}}\ge\sqrt{10}+z_{0.95}$,
$F_{*}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}\approx23.1$, $\approx24$ on the $F-1$
Nagar normalisation and $\approx26$ with $z_{0.975}=1.96$, the $F\approx20\!-\!30$
conservative inflation of the point $F\approx10$ rule.  The $16.38\approx16$
non-central $\chi^{2}$ quantile is the exact weak-instrument limit of the
inversion and is the operational Stock–Yogo benchmark used in practice.
